units.title: Economy: separate price change from output change
units.subject: Economy
units.objective: Distinguish current-price value from output valued at a fixed price base. A larger money total alone does not show how much physical production changed.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Choose the comparison
concepts.text: Distinguish current-price value from output valued at a fixed price base. A larger money total alone does not show how much physical production changed.

concepts.title: Use the index consistently
concepts.text: For a GDP deflator with base 100, real GDP = nominal GDP × 100 / deflator. Keep the base year and currency unit fixed when comparing years. This is not a live Indian GDP estimate.

concepts.title: Read the result carefully
concepts.text: For the original example below, 480 / 1.20 = 400. A prior real value of 380 gives growth 20/380, not 20/480. The price adjustment and the growth denominator are separate steps.

example.problem: An invented economy has nominal output 480 billion and GDP deflator 120. Prior-year real output on the same base was 380 billion. Find current real output and its growth.
steps: Real output = 480/1.20 = 400 billion in base-year prices.

recall: Why does an index of 120 mean division by 1.20?
Which price base must match across years?
Can nominal growth alone identify real growth?
units.mistake: Dividing by 120 instead of 1.20 loses a factor of 100. Do not substitute CPI for the GDP deflator without a stated model.

units.title: Data interpretation: choose totals and comparison bases
units.subject: Data Interpretation
units.objective: Read what each cell counts, the period and whether categories overlap. For disjoint categories, add counts before calculating a combined share.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Annotate the table
concepts.text: Read what each cell counts, the period and whether categories overlap. For disjoint categories, add counts before calculating a combined share.

concepts.title: Choose the denominator
concepts.text: A share uses the relevant total; growth uses the earlier value; a ratio compares the requested quantities. State that denominator before doing arithmetic.

concepts.title: Check an original table
concepts.text: Three fictional branches have January/February counts A:120/150, B:80/100, C:100/150. January total is 300; February total is 400. Combined growth is 100/300, not the average of 25%, 25% and 50%.

example.problem: Using A:120→150, B:80→100 and C:100→150, find total growth and C’s February share.

recall: What is the base for percentage growth?
Why can averaging branch growth rates fail?
When may cell counts be added?
units.mistake: An unweighted mean of category percentages can differ from the aggregate change. Keep the original totals visible.

units.title: Critical reasoning: necessary and sufficient conditions
units.subject: Reasoning and Comprehension
units.objective: If P then Q makes P sufficient for Q and Q necessary for P. It does not say Q is sufficient for P. Treat these as logical relations, not causal evidence.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Translate exactly
concepts.text: If P then Q makes P sufficient for Q and Q necessary for P. It does not say Q is sufficient for P. Treat these as logical relations, not causal evidence.

concepts.title: Find the forbidden case
concepts.text: P true with Q false violates P→Q. The contrapositive, not-Q→not-P, excludes that same case. Reversing the arrow generally does not.

concepts.title: Separate policy and evidence
concepts.text: Suppose every approved laboratory booking requires a completed safety induction. Induction is necessary for approval. A trained applicant may still lack equipment clearance, so training alone does not prove approval.

example.problem: Policy: every approved booking has a completed induction. Mira has no completed induction. Can Mira’s booking be approved under that policy?
steps: Let P mean approved booking and Q mean completed induction.
Mira satisfies not-Q, so approval would contradict the policy.
example.answer: No, provided the stated policy applies without exceptions.

recall: Which case falsifies P→Q?
Is its converse equivalent?
Does necessary imply sufficient?
units.mistake: Affirming the consequent: observing Q does not establish P. Also do not assume a real-world causal mechanism from a logical conditional.

units.title: AC circuits: RMS values and real power
units.subject: Electric Circuits
units.objective: For a sinusoid with peak Vm, Vrms=Vm/√2. An RMS value is not the peak or the full-cycle arithmetic average.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Name the amplitudes
concepts.text: For a sinusoid with peak Vm, Vrms=Vm/√2. An RMS value is not the peak or the full-cycle arithmetic average.

concepts.title: Track power factor
concepts.text: For sinusoidal steady-state voltage and current, average real power P=Vrms Irms cos φ. The product Vrms Irms is apparent power in VA. This simple cosine relation assumes sinusoidal waveforms.

concepts.title: Use a numerical check
concepts.text: An original load at 200 V RMS, 5 A RMS and power factor 0.8 absorbs 800 W, while its apparent power is 1000 VA. A reactive ideal element may exchange energy while its average real power is zero.

example.problem: A sinusoidal load takes 4 A RMS from 150 V RMS at power factor 0.75. Find apparent and real power.
steps: Both supplied electrical magnitudes are already RMS.
Check that P≤S for the passive load and stated power factor.

recall: How do peak and RMS differ?
When is Vrms Irms real power?
Why can zero average power coexist with current?
units.mistake: Do not multiply RMS power by an extra half. Do not use cos φ as the total power factor for arbitrary distorted waveforms.

units.title: Digital electronics: verify a Boolean function
units.subject: Digital Electronics
units.objective: Write each gate’s output for a given input before combining gates. NAND complements AND; NOR complements OR. A one at an OR input is sufficient for a one at its output.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Evaluate intermediate nodes
concepts.text: Write each gate’s output for a given input before combining gates. NAND complements AND; NOR complements OR. A one at an OR input is sufficient for a one at its output.

concepts.title: Compare every row
concepts.text: Two Boolean expressions are equivalent if their outputs agree for every input assignment. For two independent binary inputs, test 00, 01, 10 and 11.

concepts.title: Work an original function
concepts.text: For Y=(A AND B) OR (NOT A AND B), evaluate 00→0, 01→1, 10→0, 11→1. This matches B. A changes which product term is active but never changes the final output for fixed B.

example.problem: Evaluate Y=NAND(A,B) at A=1,B=1, then compare with Y when A=0,B=1.
steps: At 11, AND is 1. Complement it to get NAND=0.
At 01, AND is 0. Complement it to get NAND=1.
The change follows the truth table, not ordinary arithmetic on the output label.

recall: When is a NAND output zero?
How many rows have n binary inputs?
What evidence proves equivalence?
units.mistake: An inversion bubble changes the function. Do not replace NAND with AND or mistake a Boolean OR for addition of unrestricted integers.

units.title: Instrumentation: strain, gauge factor and bridge balance
units.subject: Measurements and Instrumentation
units.objective: Engineering strain ε=ΔL/L is dimensionless. One microstrain is 10⁻⁶ strain. Keep length units identical before dividing.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Convert strain units
concepts.text: Engineering strain ε=ΔL/L is dimensionless. One microstrain is 10⁻⁶ strain. Keep length units identical before dividing.

concepts.title: Apply gauge factor
concepts.text: For the stated linear resistive model, GF=(ΔR/R)/ε, so ΔR=GF×ε×R. The sign records tension or compression for a positive gauge factor.

concepts.title: Separate sensor and circuit
concepts.text: An original 200 Ω gauge with GF=2 at 250 microstrain changes by 0.1 Ω. A Wheatstone bridge converts resistance imbalance to voltage. Output sign depends on arm placement and voltage polarity, so no unstated sign convention is assumed here.

example.problem: A 350 Ω gauge with GF=2 sees +400 microstrain. Find its resistance change and final resistance in the linear model.

recall: Why is strain dimensionless?
Where does the factor 10⁻⁶ enter?
What determines bridge output polarity?
units.mistake: Microstrain is not percent strain. A gauge-factor formula alone does not determine bridge output voltage or temperature compensation.

units.title: Electrical machines: ideal transformer ratios
units.subject: Electrical Machines
units.objective: For the ideal transformer voltage magnitudes, Vs/Vp=Ns/Np. A larger secondary turns count raises the voltage magnitude for the stated alternating operation.
units.review: Original worked lesson with author checks. No independent human editorial review; not a complete exam chapter.

concepts.title: Fix the winding labels
concepts.text: For the ideal transformer voltage magnitudes, Vs/Vp=Ns/Np. A larger secondary turns count raises the voltage magnitude for the stated alternating operation.

concepts.title: Use ideal power balance
concepts.text: With losses neglected, Vp Ip=Vs Is for the corresponding load power conditions. Current magnitudes change inversely with the turns ratio. This ideal model does not describe saturation, inrush or leakage.

concepts.title: Refer impedance consistently
concepts.text: For a resistive secondary load RL, its primary-referred value is (Np/Ns)² RL. An original 4:1 turns ratio maps 5 Ω to 80 Ω. Referring a quantity is not physically changing the resistor.

example.problem: An ideal transformer has Np=800, Ns=200 and Vp=240 V RMS. A 6 Ω resistive load is connected to the secondary. Find Vs, Is, Ip and primary-referred resistance.
steps: Voltage ratio gives Vs=240×200/800=60 V RMS.
The resistive secondary current is Is=60/6=10 A RMS.
Ideal power balance gives Ip=60×10/240=2.5 A RMS.

recall: Which ratio scales voltage?
Why is current inversely scaled?
Why is impedance scaled by a squared ratio?
units.mistake: Do not apply the voltage ratio in the same direction to current. The ideal model cannot be used as a safe design for mains hardware.

questions.stem: An invented economy has nominal GDP 660 and deflator 110 (base 100). What is real GDP in the same units?
Nominal GDP is 900 and real GDP is 750 on one price base. What is the base-100 GDP deflator?
Nominal output rises 10% and the GDP deflator rises 10% on a common base. What happens to real output?
Real GDP rises from 400 to 420 on the same base. What is its percentage growth?
Which comparison can isolate real output growth from the supplied GDP figures?
questions.explanation: Both figures must be valued on a common price base.
options: Current nominal GDP and an unrelated CPI only
Two nominal GDP totals without prices
Two real GDP totals using the same price base

questions.stem: Nominal GDP is 450 and the deflator is 90 (base 100). Find real GDP.
questions.explanation: 450 × 100/90 = 500. A deflator below 100 makes the fixed-base value larger than this nominal value.

questions.stem: What is the February total?
questions.context: Original fictional branch counts, January / February: A 120 / 150; B 80 / 100; C 100 / 150. Counts are disjoint and use the same definition in both months.

questions.stem: What percentage of the February total is C?
questions.context: Original fictional branch counts, January / February: A 120 / 150; B 80 / 100; C 100 / 150. Counts are disjoint and use the same definition in both months.

questions.stem: What is B’s January count as a percentage of A’s January count? Enter to two decimal places.
questions.context: Original fictional branch counts, January / February: A 120 / 150; B 80 / 100; C 100 / 150. Counts are disjoint and use the same definition in both months.

questions.stem: How many more cases did C record in February than January?
questions.context: Original fictional branch counts, January / February: A 120 / 150; B 80 / 100; C 100 / 150. Counts are disjoint and use the same definition in both months.

questions.stem: What is A’s percentage increase from January to February?
questions.context: Original fictional branch counts, January / February: A 120 / 150; B 80 / 100; C 100 / 150. Counts are disjoint and use the same definition in both months.

questions.stem: Which branch has the largest percentage increase from January to February?
questions.explanation: A and B each grow 25%; C grows 50%.
questions.context: Original fictional branch counts, January / February: A 120 / 150; B 80 / 100; C 100 / 150. Counts are disjoint and use the same definition in both months.

questions.stem: All approved lab bookings require induction. Asha completed induction. What follows about her approval?
questions.explanation: Induction is necessary but may not be sufficient.
options: Approval cannot be determined from this alone

questions.stem: Which is equivalent to “If a file is accepted, it has a valid signature”?
options: If it lacks a valid signature, it is not accepted
If it has a valid signature, it is accepted
If it is rejected, it lacks a valid signature

questions.stem: For the statement P→Q, which assignments make the implication true?
A permit is issued only if the fee is paid. Which condition is necessary for issuance?
questions.explanation: Only if introduces the necessary condition.
options: A permit has already been issued
Every fee payer receives a permit

questions.stem: For two Boolean propositions P and Q, how many truth assignments falsify P→Q? Enter an integer.
questions.explanation: Only P=true,Q=false, out of the four assignments.

questions.stem: Every red token is round. A token is not round. What follows?
questions.explanation: The contrapositive excludes redness when roundness is absent.

questions.stem: A sinusoidal load has 240 V RMS, 2 A RMS and power factor 0.6. Find average real power in W.
A sinusoidal voltage has peak 100√2 V. What is its RMS value in V?
A passive sinusoidal load takes 300 W at 100 V RMS and 5 A RMS. What is its power factor?
An ideal inductor in sinusoidal steady state absorbs what average real power over a whole cycle?
questions.explanation: Its voltage and current differ in phase by 90°, so cos φ=0.

questions.stem: For a passive sinusoidal load, which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Real power is VI cosφ; apparent power is VI; RMS is peak/√2 for a sine.
options: RMS voltage always equals its peak

questions.stem: A purely resistive sinusoidal load has 50 V RMS and 2 A RMS. Find its average real power in W.
questions.explanation: Voltage and current are in phase, so P=50×2=100 W.

questions.stem: What is the output of a two-input NAND gate for inputs 1 and 1?
What is the output of a two-input NOR gate for inputs 0 and 0?
How many input rows are required for a complete truth table with three independent binary inputs?
questions.explanation: Each of three inputs has two choices: 2³=8.

questions.stem: The Boolean expression (A AND B) OR (NOT A AND B) equals which function?
questions.explanation: Factor B: B AND (A OR NOT A)=B.

questions.stem: For a two-input AND gate, which input pairs give output zero?
questions.explanation: AND is one only when both inputs are one.

questions.stem: For two independent binary inputs, how many rows have a two-input OR output equal to 1?
A 200 Ω resistive gauge has GF=2 and strain +500 microstrain. Find ΔR in Ω using the linear model.
A 100 mm bar elongates by 0.02 mm. What is the strain in microstrain?
A gauge has ΔR/R=0.001 and strain 500 microstrain. Find its gauge factor.
Which quantity is engineering strain ΔL/L?
questions.explanation: The same length unit cancels between numerator and denominator.

questions.stem: A 120 Ω gauge with positive GF=2 experiences −1000 microstrain. Find its final resistance in Ω in the linear model.
Which statements about the stated linear resistive-gauge model are correct?
questions.explanation: Both follow the definition; other claims require circuit/configuration details.
options: Gauge factor alone determines bridge output polarity
Any single active gauge always cancels all temperature effects

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has Np=1000, Ns=250 and Vp=200 V RMS. Find Vs in V RMS.
An ideal transformer delivers 100 V RMS at 4 A RMS into a resistive load. At 200 V RMS primary voltage, find primary current in A RMS.
questions.explanation: Secondary power=400 W; ideal primary current=400/200=2 A.

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has Np/Ns=3 and a 4 Ω resistive secondary load. Find the primary-referred resistance in Ω.
For an ideal step-up transformer supplying a resistive load, which relation holds for current magnitudes?
questions.explanation: Power balance and raised voltage imply a smaller secondary current than primary.
options: Secondary current is smaller than primary current
Both currents must always be equal

questions.stem: An ideal transformer has Ns/Np=0.2 and secondary current 5 A RMS into a resistive load. Find primary current in A RMS.
Which are assumptions or consequences of the ideal transformer model used here?
questions.explanation: Losslessness and the voltage ratio are ideal-model statements; real behaviour has additional effects.
options: No winding or core power loss in the model
It accurately predicts all inrush currents
Voltage magnitude ratio equals turns ratio
It permits arbitrary DC steady-state operation without magnetic limitations
